opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think that's one of the hardest things about this job, and I'm not sure anyone fully solves it. When you start out, you don't know which problems are supposed to be hard, which approaches have supposedly been tried and failed, which questions the field has quietly decided aren't interesting anymore. That ignorance is a real asset. A lot of the best work I've seen from students comes from them not knowing they weren't supposed to try something.

The longer you're around, the more you accumulate these little heuristics, things like "oh, that never works," or "people tried that in the nineties," and most of the time those heuristics are useful. They save you from wasting six months. But they also go stale, especially in a field that's moved as fast as ours has in the last several years. Things that genuinely didn't work at one scale, or with one kind of model, suddenly do work, and if you're carrying around old priors, you're the last person to notice.

So the main thing I try to do is lean on my students. They're the ones who show up without those assumptions, and a big part of my role is to not squash that. When a student comes in with an idea and my first instinct is "that won't work," I try to treat that instinct with some suspicion and ask, why do I believe that? Is it because I've seen evidence recently, or because it was true when I was a grad student? Pretty often it's the second one.

The other thing is just deliberately working on problems where I'm not an expert. If you keep returning to the same set of questions, you get deeper but also more entrenched. Moving into adjacent areas, whether that's talking to people in cognitive science or linguistics or working on some new interpretability or alignment question, puts you back in the position of not knowing what the received wisdom is. That discomfort is kind of the point.

I don't think you ever get all the way back to being a first-year student. But you can build habits and surround yourself with people that keep you from getting too comfortable, and I think that's about the best you can do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses accumulated assumptions becoming stale and ways to question them, but it does not say unlearning assumptions takes much longer than learning them.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think about it more than I'd like to admit. I don't think you ever fully get that back. Once you've spent years building up a set of intuitions about what works and what doesn't, those intuitions are useful, but they're also a kind of cage. You start pattern-matching new ideas onto old ones and dismissing things too quickly because they resemble something that failed in 2016.

The honest answer is that the best mechanism I've found is students. A first-year PhD student walks in with a question that I would never have asked, because I "know" the answer, and about one time in five it turns out that what I knew was wrong, or was only true under conditions that no longer hold. Language models have been very humbling in that respect. A lot of the structural assumptions my generation had, about what you'd need to build in explicitly, compositionality, grounding, modularity, just didn't turn out to be prerequisites in the way we expected. So I try to treat my own confident beliefs as hypotheses that are due for re-testing, and I try to surround myself with people who haven't absorbed them yet.

The other thing I'd say is that some of the burden is actually valuable. New researchers are flexible partly because they haven't yet learned which problems are hard for deep reasons versus hard for incidental ones. What I'd like to keep is the ability to tell those apart, while being much more willing to go back and check whether the "deep reasons" are still deep. I'm not sure I succeed at that, but it's what I aim for.

r001.rationale: The response says established intuitions are hard to shed and may never be fully overcome, but it does not state that unlearning assumptions takes much longer than learning them.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s something you have to work at. Once you’ve spent a long time thinking about a problem in a particular way, it becomes easy to mistake the assumptions that made your approach useful for facts about the problem itself.

One of the things I really like about working with students is that they haven’t necessarily internalized those assumptions. They’ll ask, “Why are we doing it this way?” And sometimes there’s a good answer, but sometimes the answer is just that this is how we’ve been doing it. Taking those questions seriously is one way to keep some of that flexibility.

I don’t know that I can get back to being a completely new researcher, and I wouldn’t want to give up everything I’ve learned. But I’d like to get better at recognizing when that experience is helping me and when it’s narrowing the set of questions I’m willing to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says it takes effort to notice and question established assumptions, but does not state that unlearning them takes much longer than learning them.

sol-6.1.text:
I hope some of that flexibility comes from working with students. They come in without necessarily sharing my intuitions about which problems are interesting or which approaches ought to work, and they ask questions that make me realize I’ve been treating something as settled when it really isn’t.

But there’s a tension there, because part of my job is to offer guidance based on experience. You don’t want to discard everything you’ve learned just to feel intellectually young. The thing I’d like to get better at is distinguishing between having a reason to think something won’t work and simply having seen people do things a different way. And then giving students—and myself—enough room to try the thing anyway.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how experience can make assumptions feel settled and the challenge of staying open, but does not say that unlearning established assumptions takes much longer than learning them.
